newsitem.title: USA: Fed may be inching to rate hike but timing unclear.
newsitem.headline: Fed may be inching to rate hike but timing unclear.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent

The Federal Reserve may be inching toward raising interest rates for the first time in two years, but it remains an open question whether it will finally make the move this month, officials and Fed watchers said.
"It's hard to tell," one central bank official, who declined to be named, said.
While the economy does not look to be overheating, it is still bubbling along at a level that makes Fed policymakers fret about the risk of inflation popping up.
So far, though, there are scant signs of that happening. The economy created a whopping 339,000 jobs last month, but wages on average only rose by 3 cents an hour, to $12.09.
"Labor markets seem to be on the taut side but it does not appear to be showing greatly through to worker compensation yet," one central bank official said.
That leaves Fed policymakers in the same quandary that they have been for months.
History tells them that inflation will eventually rise when labor markets are as tight as they are now, as workers demand -- and get -- fatter paychecks. But that does not seem to be happening yet.

Joel Prakken, Chairman of St. Louis-based Macroeconomic Advisers, said that the Fed may eventually nudge interest rates up to rebalance the inflationary risks in the economy, but he doubted that would happen this month.
The central bank's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) holds its next meeting on March 25.

It has not changed short-term rates since Jan. 31, 1996, when it cut the federal funds rate that banks charge each other for money to 5.25 percent, from 5.5, and the discount rate it charges banks for loans to 5.0 percent from 5.25.
A group of four Democratic Party lawmakers on Monday urged the central bank not to raise rates unless there are clear signs of inflation.

"Unless specific and definite signs of inflation can be sighted, we strongly urge you and the Federal Open Market Committee to resist any action that could lead to higher interest rates," Senators Tom Harkin of Iowa, Byron Dorgan of North Dakota and Jack Reed of Rhode Island and Representative Maurice Hinchey of New York said in a letter to Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan.

Fed officials said that the recent departure of Janet Yellen from the FOMC for a top post at the White House robbed the central bank of a policymaker who had been willing to challenge those in the institution arguing for higher rates.
But it is by no means clear that her departure -- and that of Fed Governor Lawrence Lindsey for the private sector -- will be enough to tip the scales in the direction of a rate hike.

Despite a string of stronger-than-expected economic statistics last week, the economy is expected to slow in the first quarter from its torrid fourth quarter pace, when surging exports pushed growth to an annualized 3.9 percent.

"The economy at this particular stage in time ... is clearly running very close to any measure of capacity," Greenspan said last week. "It is not one that is clearly overheated, one in which inflation is clearly accelerating."
Greenpsan though went on to say that the inflationary risks remain on the upside, as they have been for months.

On the face of it, Fed policymakers would seem to risk little by nudging rates higher at this time. The economy remains buoyant and a small rate rise on its own would not put much of a crimp in growth.
But Fed policymakers are aware that any move now could have more of an impact because it would represent a reversal of policy.
The effect of a rate increase on the high-flying stock market remains uncertain as well. Greenspan warned earlier this month that equity prices may be too high.

The Fed is worried that a steep, unwarranted rise in stock prices could lead to a surge in consumer spending as investors spend some of their gains. But so far, the so-called "wealth effect" from the market's rise has been less than expected.
